Series::acosh¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::acosh() const -> Series
Series& Series::acosh_()

What It Does¶

acosh() applies the inverse hyperbolic cosine elementwise. If y=acosh(x), then cosh(y)=x and the principal result satisfies y>=0.

Unlike an ordinary inverse cosine, this method does not return an angle. Hyperbolic functions parameterize the unit hyperbola; acosh() recovers the nonnegative hyperbolic coordinate whose cosh() value is the input.

Recovering A Nonnegative Hyperbolic Coordinate¶

Real hyperbolic cosine never falls below one. The real domain is therefore x>=1. The boundary value acosh(1)=0 is valid, while values below one return nan. This domain is the first condition to check when acosh() appears after roundoff-prone arithmetic.

The operation is elementwise: shape is preserved, dimensions do not interact, and no reduction or broadcasting occurs.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series A new shape-preserving Series. Floating inputs retain their floating dtype. Bool, integral, and float8 inputs promote to a supported floating dtype because inverse hyperbolic values are generally fractional.

Gradient¶

For x>1,

d acosh(x) / dx = 1 / sqrt(x^2 - 1)

The derivative is positive and becomes unbounded as x approaches 1 from above. The forward boundary is valid, but it is not a numerically gentle point for gradient-based work.

In-Place Form¶

acosh_() is the in-place sibling of acosh(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 5.0});

auto& ref = x.acosh_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1.3169579, 2.2924317]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Values produced by cosh() map back to their nonnegative inputs.

auto values = pluss::make_series({
    1.0,
    1.5430806348152437,
    3.7621956910836314,
});
std::cout << values.acosh() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 2]

Example 2. The domain boundary and a violation remain visible in the result.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0}).acosh() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, 0, 1.3169579]

Example 3. Reverse mode follows the analytic interior derivative.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.25, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.acosh().sum().reverse();
std::cout << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.3333333, 0.57735027]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Real inputs below 1 produce nan.

  • The derivative diverges at the valid boundary x=1.

  • This is an inverse hyperbolic function, not an angle-producing inverse trigonometric function.

  • The method is out-of-place; the separate acosh_() surface mutates.

Summary¶

Use acosh() to recover nonnegative hyperbolic coordinates from values in [1,infinity). Guard the lower domain boundary when gradients matter.

Aliases¶

arccosh() / arccosh_() — spelling is kept for torch-style naming familiarity. Each resolves to exactly the same dispatch as acosh() / acosh_() before any computation runs, so behavior, gradient, and failure modes are identical; nothing here is a separate implementation to learn.
